stimulus.title: A car over a hill
stimulus.html: A car of mass m drives over the crest of a hill at a constant speed v. Near the crest the road follows a vertical circle of radius R. Air resistance and the friction along the direction of motion balance, so the speed stays constant.

drawSpec.label: A dot that stands for the car at the crest of the hill; draw each force on it as an arrow starting on the dot

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Draw a free-body diagram of the car at the top of the crest, showing only the vertical forces. Represent each force with a distinct arrow starting on the dot, labeled with its type and agent, with lengths that show their relative sizes.

rubric.point: Gravitational force down, labeled (F_g, Earth on car)
Normal force up, labeled (F_N, road on car)
accept: road pushes up on the car

rubric.point: F_N drawn shorter than F_g, and no "centripetal force" or net force arrow
accept: normal force arrow visibly shorter, with only two arrows

parts.sample: Two arrows start on the dot: F_g (Earth on car) pointing down, and F_N (road on car) pointing up, drawn shorter than F_g. No centripetal or net force arrow is drawn: the net force toward the center is the difference between these two.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the normal force on the car at the crest in terms of m, v, R and physical constants, consistent with your free-body diagram.

rubric.point: Newton's second law with the centripetal acceleration v²/R toward the center (down)

parts.sample: Newton's second law toward the center of the circle, which is below the car: ΣF = ma_c with a_c = v²/R. The forces toward the center are F_g = mg (down, toward) and F_N (up, away): mg − F_N = mv²/R. So F_N = m(g − v²/R) = mg − (m/R)v².

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Sketch a graph of the normal force on the car at the crest against v², for speeds from zero up to the speed at which the normal force becomes zero. Label the intercepts in terms of m, g and R.

rubric.point: A straight line with negative slope

parts.sample: A straight line that starts at F_N = mg on the vertical axis (v² = 0) and falls with slope −m/R, reaching F_N = 0 at v² = gR on the horizontal axis.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The driver goes over the crest faster than √(gR). Predict what happens to the car at the crest, and explain how your free-body diagram, your equation and your graph each support the prediction.

rubric.point: Predicts the car leaves the road (loses contact) at the crest
accept: the tires lift off; the car becomes airborne

rubric.point: Equation/graph: F_N = m(g − v²/R) would be negative for v² > gR, beyond the graph's horizontal intercept, but a road can only push, not pull
accept: the line crosses zero at v² = gR

rubric.point: Free-body diagram: gravity is the only force left and mg is smaller than the mv²/R needed to follow the circle, so the car's path curves less than the road
accept: gravity alone cannot supply the needed centripetal net force

parts.sample: The car leaves the road at the crest. My equation gives F_N = m(g − v²/R), which is negative for v² > gR: the graph has crossed its horizontal intercept. A road can only push up on the car, so it cannot supply a negative normal force; F_N drops to zero. With only F_g left on the free-body diagram, the net force toward the center is mg, smaller than the mv²/R needed to follow a circle of radius R, so the car follows a flatter path than the road and lifts off.
